Even "play Clip.mp3" returns 'choose'. `_matches` (player.py:38-45) also compares `Path(query).stem` ("clip") against each file's stem, so Clip.wav matches the full mp3 filename too. The "Play now" button in the generation dialog is not affected because it uses the returned audio_url directly. Only the chat "play ..." shortcut, the registry tool and the `/tts/files` search are affected.

The disk estimate holds. `SAMPLE_RATE` is 24000 and the WAV is PCM_16 mono, so 48 KB/s, about 173 MB per hour. A failed ffmpeg run also leaves the orphan WAV behind.

The suggestion's note about deduplication is accurate. `_build_filename_stem` (:151) only checks whether `<stem>.wav` exists. If the fix deletes the intermediate WAV without also changing that check to look at the target extension, a second mp3 with the same title would silently overwrite the first.
findings.status_note: The intermediate WAV is built in a temporary directory, so only the final file reaches local_storage/audio.

findings.title: KOKORO_CACHE_DIR is ignored in the running app: HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE is set after huggingface_hub is already imported
findings.detail: `os.environ.setdefault("HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE", ...)` only takes effect if huggingface_hub.constants hasn't been imported yet. agent.py:6 imports core.speech_to_text (faster_whisper -> huggingface_hub, and it instantiates WhisperModel at import) before agent.py:12 imports features.audio.player -> text_to_speech. I verified the import order (['core.agent_routes','agent','core.speech_to_text','faster_whisper','huggingface_hub','features.audio.player','features.audio.text_to_speech',...]). After `import core.ui`, huggingface_hub.constants.HF_HUB_CACHE resolves to ~/.cache/huggingface/hub. As a result, ~/.cache/huggingface/hub contains models--hexgrad--Kokoro-82M while models/kokoro contains both Kokoro and models--Systran--faster-whisper-base. Weights are downloaded twice depending on which module imports first, the env override leaks into Whisper, and README's `KOKORO_CACHE_DIR` default of models/kokoro is not honored.
findings.suggestion: Don't rely on process env set at audio-module import time. Either set HF_HUB_CACHE (or KOKORO_CACHE_DIR) in a small config module imported first by core/ui.py and agent.py, or download explicitly with huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download(repo_id, filename, cache_dir=KOKORO_CACHE_DIR) and build KModel(config=..., model=...) / load voices from those paths. Also pass repo_id='hexgrad/Kokoro-82M' to KPipeline to silence its warning.
findings.verification_note:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. Every step of the failure checks out:
(1) features/audio/text_to_speech.py:39 sets HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE with os.environ.setdefault while the module is being imported. huggingface_hub reads that variable only once, when huggingface_hub.constants is first imported (constants.py:171-179 in v1.29.0). After that, hf_hub_download falls back to constants.HF_HUB_CACHE whenever cache_dir is None (file_download.py:977-978).
(2) Kokoro 0.9.4 calls hf_hub_download without cache_dir in kokoro/model.py:46 and 67 and kokoro/pipeline.py:142, so the frozen constant decides where its files go.
(3) In both entry points, huggingface_hub is imported before text_to_speech. core/ui.py:10 imports core.agent_routes, which imports agent, and agent.py:6 imports core.speech_to_text, which imports faster_whisper and with it huggingface_hub. features.audio.player is not imported until agent.py:12. I checked this read-only with all HF env vars unset:
- `import core.ui` gives HF_HUB_CACHE=/home/hms/.cache/huggingface/hub, even though os.environ['HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE'] now holds .../models/kokoro.
- `import agent` (the CLI path) gives the same ~/.cache result.
- Only `import features.audio.text_to_speech` on its own resolves to models/kokoro.
(4) The disk shows the result. The Kokoro weights (config.json, kokoro-v1_0.pth, voices) exist in both ~/.cache/huggingface/hub and models/kokoro, and models/kokoro also holds a copy of models--Systran--faster-whisper-base.
Nothing in the code prevents this. Nothing passes cache_dir, and the only references to KOKORO_CACHE_DIR or HF cache variables are text_to_speech.py:34-39 and README.md:87,94. No test checks where the cache goes. README's documented default (KOKORO_CACHE_DIR = models/kokoro) is therefore not honored in the web app or the CLI.
One detail needs tightening. In the web app and CLI, Whisper does not pick up the override inside the same process, because WhisperModel is created at speech_to_text.py:9, before line 39 runs. The leak into Whisper only happens when text_to_speech is imported before huggingface_hub, for example when the audio modules are imported on their own. Child processes also inherit the variable. That is the likely source of the Whisper copy in models/kokoro. Low severity is right: the effect is duplicate downloads and a setting that does nothing, not broken behavior. The suggested fix is sound: pass cache_dir explicitly to hf_hub_download and build KModel / load voices from those paths, or set the cache variable in a module that is imported first.

findings.title: Kokoro pipeline creation and use have no lock while requests run in a thread pool
findings.detail: _get_pipeline does an unlocked check-then-set on the module-level _pipelines dict. /tts and /tts/dialogue run synthesize in Starlette's thread pool (routes.py:72, 145), so two requests arriving before the first pipeline exists will each build a KPipeline (KModel of about 82M params plus an EspeakFallback): double load time and memory, with one copy thrown away. After that, concurrent requests drive the same KPipeline from several threads (g2p with espeak fallback, the self.voices cache dict, the torch model). Kokoro doesn't document that as thread-safe, and on CPU each torch call already uses every core, so parallel runs oversubscribe. Whether this corrupts output is plausible but not reproduced. The double load follows directly from the code.
findings.suggestion: Add a module-level threading.Lock. Hold it around pipeline creation, and probably around the whole _synthesize_kokoro call so requests are processed one at a time (simplest, and matches the single-user design). Alternatively, run synthesis on a dedicated single-worker executor.
findings.verification_note:
I traced the code and the finding holds. features/audio/text_to_speech.py:199-205 `_get_pipeline` checks and then sets the module-level `_pipelines` dict (line 158) with no lock. Nothing in core/ or features/ warms the pipeline at startup and nothing else guards it. Both synthesis routes hand off to Starlette's thread pool: features/audio/routes.py:72 (`synthesize`) and :145 (`synthesize_dialogue`). Both reach `_synthesize_kokoro` (line 227), which calls `_get_pipeline`. Every voice in KOKORO_VOICES uses lang_code "b", so all requests share a single KPipeline.

I reproduced the double construction read-only. I put a fake `kokoro` module with a slow `KPipeline.__init__` into sys.modules and called `t._get_pipeline('b')` from two threads. Output: "constructions: 2 distinct objects returned: 2". One copy is thrown away, and the two callers end up holding different pipeline objects.

In the installed kokoro (venv/.../kokoro/pipeline.py), `__init__` builds `KModel(...).to(device).eval()` at line 99 and an `EspeakFallback` at line 108. `self.voices` is an unlocked check-then-set cache (lines 137-148 and 160-166). So concurrent use of the shared pipeline is real, though I did not reproduce any corrupted output, which matches what the reviewer said. The tests do not cover this: tests/test_text_to_speech.py:106-114 monkeypatches `_get_pipeline` and `_pipelines` with a fake.

One caveat on how easily it triggers. The only frontend caller (features/audio/static/tts.js:260/304) disables the Generate button while a request is in flight, so one tab cannot start two synthesis requests at once. It does need two tabs, direct API calls, or a page reload during a slow first model load. A reload works because the run_in_threadpool job keeps running on the server after the client goes away, and a second submit then starts a second KPipeline build. Single-user use reaches it this way, so "low" severity is right.

The suggested lock around the whole `synthesize`/`synthesize_dialogue` body would also close a related small race. The `_build_filename_stem` exists-then-write check (lines 150-153, called at 336/422) uses minute-precision default names, so two jobs finishing in the same minute could overwrite each other's file.

findings.title: Upload size caps don't limit disk use: Starlette writes the whole upload to temp storage before the handler checks
findings.detail: The comment says MAX_CONVERT_FILE_BYTES is "small enough that an upload can't fill the disk", and there is a similar 20 MB cap for /tts/extract-text. But routes.py:90/116 call `await request.form()`. Starlette's MultiPartParser (verified in the installed 1.6.0 source) applies max_part_size only to non-file fields; file parts go into a SpooledTemporaryFile that spills to disk with no limit. A multi-GB upload is therefore received and written to the system temp dir in full, and only then does _save_upload_bounded reject it, after copying another 100 MB. Separately, convert_audio_file writes its input into AUDIO_DIR as upload_<ts>.<ext>. While ffmpeg runs, that file shows up in /tts/files and in the play list, and it is left behind if the process dies. The routes require login, so the risk is limited to an authenticated user.
findings.suggestion: Before `await request.form()`, reject requests whose Content-Length is over the cap plus a small multipart allowance (413), and handle missing or chunked lengths by reading request.stream() with a running byte count. Save the converter's input to tempfile instead of AUDIO_DIR, as extract_text_from_document already does.
findings.verification_note:
The core mechanism is real, and I reproduced it. In the installed Starlette 1.6.0, formparsers.py:181-188 enforces max_part_size only when `_current_part.file is None`. File parts go into `SpooledTemporaryFile(max_size=1MB)` (line 230), which then grows without limit (line 284). A TestClient POST carrying a 5 MB file part was accepted (200), while a 2 MB plain field was rejected with 400 "Field exceeded maximum size of 1024KB". So the comment at features/audio/text_to_speech.py:88-90, "small enough that an upload can't fill the disk", is false: routes.py:90 and :116 call `await request.form()`, the whole body is spooled first, and only then does `_save_upload_bounded` (text_to_speech.py:429-444) copy up to another 100 MB or 20 MB and reject it. The secondary claim also holds: `convert_audio_file` writes `AUDIO_DIR/upload_<ts>.<ext>` (line 461). Its extension is limited to wav/mp3/flac/ogg, which are exactly player.py's AUDIO_EXTENSIONS, so during ffmpeg the file is listed by /tts/files, served at /audio/, and left behind if the process is killed (the `finally` at line 470 never runs).

Several details are wrong or understated.
(1) "Requires login" is not the boundary. The audio routes do reject unauthenticated callers before the body is read: they take only a Request, so `is_logged_in` raises first, and my unauthenticated /tts/convert test got a 303. But POST /login (core/auth.py:35) takes `password: str = Form(...)`. FastAPI (routing.py:429-431) therefore runs `await request.form()` before any check, and it accepts extra file parts of any size. The same unbounded spooling is reachable with no authentication at all. /tts (routes.py:64) and /tts/dialogue (:136) would spool attached file parts the same way.
(2) The login guard itself can be bypassed. core/ui.py:32-35 sets `SessionMiddleware(secret_key="THIS_SECRET")` as a hardcoded value. I signed `{"authenticated": true}` with itsdangerous using that key, and GET /tts/voices returned 200. Anyone who can reach the port can therefore reach every "login-required" route. This should be its own finding.
(3) On this machine /tmp is tmpfs (30 GB, RAM-backed). The spool exhausts RAM and swap rather than "the disk". It is transient: the files are unlinked, and the spool is freed when the form is closed (FastAPI closes it for /login).
(4) The default bind is 127.0.0.1 (README), so exposure requires local or LAN reachability. Low severity is appropriate.

A fix that only checks Content-Length inside the audio handlers would leave /login exposed. The limit belongs in an app-wide ASGI middleware that caps the request body by Content-Length and a running stream count.
findings.corrected:
In Starlette 1.6.0, multipart file parts are spooled to a SpooledTemporaryFile with no size limit; max_part_size only covers non-file fields. Any multipart request body is therefore received and stored in full before app code runs. On this machine /tmp is tmpfs, so this means RAM/swap exhaustion. The storage is transient and freed when the form closes.

The size caps in features/audio/text_to_speech.py:88-94 (MAX_CONVERT_FILE_BYTES, MAX_DOCUMENT_FILE_BYTES) only take effect after the full upload has been spooled. They do not stop large uploads, so the comment at line 88-89 is wrong.

The problem is not limited to authenticated audio routes:
- The unauthenticated POST /login (core/auth.py:35, `password: str = Form(...)`) makes FastAPI call request.form() before any check, and it accepts file parts of any size (verified: a 5 MB file part is accepted, while a 2 MB plain field is rejected).
- The login guard on /tts/convert, /tts/extract-text, /tts and /tts/dialogue can be bypassed, because core/ui.py:34 hardcodes the session secret as "THIS_SECRET". A forged `{"authenticated": true}` cookie was verified to return 200 on /tts/voices.

Separately, convert_audio_file (text_to_speech.py:461) writes its input to AUDIO_DIR as upload_<ts>.<wav|mp3|flac|ogg>. While ffmpeg runs, that file is visible in /tts/files and at /audio/, and it is left behind if the process is killed.

Severity is low for the default 127.0.0.1 bind and higher if the server is exposed on a network.

Suggested fixes:
- Add an app-wide ASGI middleware that rejects bodies over a cap with 413, checking Content-Length and keeping a running count over the stream for chunked or missing lengths. This also covers /login.
- Replace the hardcoded session secret with one from an environment variable or a generated value.
- Spool converter input to tempfile instead of AUDIO_DIR.

findings.title: Saved-file search writes unescaped filenames into innerHTML, and audio URLs are not percent-encoded
findings.detail: renderSavedAudioResults builds `` and assigns it to results.innerHTML. The filenames come straight from the directory listing (routes.py:59). The TTS title sanitizer limits only names this app generates; it does not limit what is on disk. write_file can write anywhere inside the project, including local_storage/audio (tools/files.py:_safe_path), and users drop files there by hand. A file named `.mp3` runs script in the app's origin when the user searches for "img". The chat path (audio-player.js) escapes the same data, so the two paths are inconsistent. Related: audio_url is built by string concatenation (`f"/audio/{f.name}"` in player.py:63/109/120 and routes.py:59), so names containing '#', '?' or '%' break. For example, 'Track #1.mp3' requests /audio/Track%20 and the rest becomes a URL fragment, giving a 404.
findings.suggestion: Build the buttons with document.createElement and textContent, or reuse escapeAudioText from audio-player.js. Build audio_url server-side with urllib.parse.quote(f.name) in one shared helper in player.py, and use it from routes.py as well.
findings.verification_note: The code defect is real and in the right place. In features/audio/static/tts.js lines 405-408, renderSavedAudioResults puts `${f.filename}` into results.innerHTML without escaping. The filename comes straight from /tts/files (features/audio/routes.py:59), which is just find_audio_files() → AUDIO_DIR.iterdir() (features/audio/player.py:28-35). That lookup does a substring match, so searching "img" does match `.mp3`, and an img onerror handler set through innerHTML does run. The app sends no CSP header (grep found none). The chat path does escape the same data: audio-player.js:29-49 uses escapeAudioText/escapeHtmlAttr, and audio_play.html is autoescaped by Jinja. So the inconsistency is real. The URL part is also correct. audio_url is built by string concatenation, with no percent-encoding, at player.py:63/109/120 and routes.py:59 (also in the escaped chat path). A name such as 'Track #1.mp3' makes the browser request /audio/Track%20 with '#1.mp3' as the fragment, which returns 404. Names containing '?' or a literal '%XX' break the same way. Reachability is narrower than the finding suggests. No HTTP endpoint lets anyone choose a name in local_storage/audio: - /tts and /tts/dialogue sanitize titles with `[^A-Za-z0-9 ._-]` → '_' (text_to_speech.py:133-146). - /tts/convert ignores the uploaded name and writes `upload_` / `converted_` (text_to_speech.py:461-465). - Every route sits behind is_logged_in. The LLM path through write_file is real (`_safe_path` only stops escapes from the project root), but config/settings.py:11 sets `"write_file": "ask"`, so the user has to approve it. An approved write_file can already write Python into the project, which uvicorn --reload would then execute, so this XSS adds no escalation over what that approval grants. That leaves files the user places in the folder themselves (their own music, or files unpacked from an untrusted archive or torrent that keeps the name), which still needs the user to search for a matching term. In practice this is self-XSS, a defense-in-depth and consistency fix, not something an attacker or the LLM can reach. The '#', '?' and '%' problem is a functional bug, not a security one, and it affects the chat path too, not only the dashboard.
findings.corrected: features/audio/static/tts.js:405-408 (renderSavedAudioResults) puts `f.filename` into innerHTML without escaping, unlike the chat path, which escapes it (audio-player.js:29-49, Jinja autoescape in audio_play.html). A file in local_storage/audio named like `.mp3` will run script in the app's origin (no CSP) when the user searches for a matching term in the dashboard's "Play a saved file" panel. No attacker-controlled route can create such a name: TTS titles are sanitized to [A-Za-z0-9 ._-], conversions use timestamp names, and all routes need login. The LLM can only do it through write_file, which config/settings.py marks "ask", so the user must approve it, and that approval already allows worse (writing project Python). Severity: low, defense-in-depth or self-XSS. Fix: use createElement/textContent or reuse escapeAudioText. Separately, as a functional bug rather than a security one: audio_url is built without percent-encoding in player.py:63/109/120 and routes.py:59. Names a user puts in the folder that contain '#', '?' or '%XX' (e.g. 'Track #1.mp3' → GET /audio/Track%20) return 404 in both the dashboard and the chat player. App-generated names cannot contain these characters. Fix: one helper that uses urllib.parse.quote(f.name), shared by player.py and routes.py.

findings.title: ffmpeg subprocess inherits the terminal's stdin, has no timeout, and auto-detects the input format
findings.detail: _run_ffmpeg calls subprocess.run([...], check=True, capture_output=True) without stdin=DEVNULL / -nostdin and without a timeout. When uvicorn runs in a terminal (the documented way to start it), ffmpeg inherits the TTY as stdin. It reads keystrokes as its own interactive commands and may change terminal settings. A malformed upload that makes ffmpeg stall ties up a thread-pool worker indefinitely. Also, the extension whitelist only checks the filename; ffmpeg still guesses the real format from the file contents, so a 'clip.wav' that is actually a playlist or concat file gets opened by that demuxer. Exploitability is not verified, so treat this last point as hardening. The missing-ffmpeg and non-zero-exit cases are handled correctly (they become RuntimeError), and there is no shell injection.
findings.suggestion: Add '-nostdin' (or stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL) and a timeout (for example scaled to the input size) that raises a RuntimeError on subprocess.TimeoutExpired. Pin the input demuxer from the whitelisted extension ({'wav':'wav','mp3':'mp3','flac':'flac','ogg':'ogg'} -> ['-f', fmt] before '-i'). Unlink a partial out_path when ffmpeg fails.
findings.verification_note: The core stdin problem is real, and I reproduced it. features/audio/text_to_speech.py:270 calls subprocess.run([...], check=True, capture_output=True) with no stdin argument and no -nostdin. That means ffmpeg inherits fd 0. Under uvicorn in a terminal (README.md:59/70), with or without --reload, fd 0 is the TTY: uvicorn's spawned reload worker keeps fd 0. Running the same call shape with a 'q' fed on the inherited stdin, ffmpeg printed "[q] command received. Exiting." and stopped at 1.5s of a 15s input with rc 0. So check=True does not catch it, and the truncated output would be returned as a success. With -nostdin the full input ran. No test covers this: pytest's fd capture points fd 0 at /dev/null, and test_text_to_speech.py:353 only runs a normal conversion. The finding misses that _run_ffmpeg is also the path for every MP3/OGG TTS generation (via _encode_with_ffmpeg, lines 283/293), not just /tts/convert. Three details are wrong or overstated. (1) The 'malformed upload stalls ffmpeg' reason for a timeout is unproven: inputs are local, server-named files capped by MAX_CONVERT_FILE_BYTES, and nothing showed a hang. The realistic hang comes from stdin itself: if uvicorn runs as a background job in a job-control shell, ffmpeg's tcsetattr/read on the TTY gets SIGTTOU/SIGTTIN. ffmpeg is then stopped, and subprocess.run (inside run_in_threadpool, routes.py:72/98/145) blocks that worker and request forever. (2) The 'playlist' demuxer claim is wrong for the installed ffmpeg n9.0.2. HLS content under a non-.m3u8 name is refused ("Not detecting m3u8/hls with non standard extension"), and file-backed SDP is blocked by the protocol whitelist. (3) Content sniffing does pick the concat demuxer for an 'ffconcat version 1.0' body, but the default safe=1 rejects absolute paths ("Unsafe file name '/etc/hostname'"). Relative names resolve inside local_storage/audio/, so a crafted upload can only pull in other audio files from the same single-user store. Pinning -f is reasonable hardening with negligible impact. Severity low is right; location line 270 is right.
findings.corrected: features/audio/text_to_speech.py:268-274 (_run_ffmpeg) runs ffmpeg without -nostdin or stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL. It is used both by /tts/convert (convert_audio_file, line 469) and by every MP3/OGG TTS output (_encode_with_ffmpeg, lines 283/293). ffmpeg therefore inherits uvicorn's stdin, which is the TTY in the documented foreground `uvicorn core.ui:app [--reload]` setup. While a conversion runs, ffmpeg switches the terminal to non-echo/non-canonical mode and reads keystrokes as commands. A stray 'q' (verified) makes it stop early with exit code 0, so check=True passes and a truncated file is returned as a success. If uvicorn is started as a background job in a job-control shell, ffmpeg is stopped by SIGTTOU/SIGTTIN. Because subprocess.run has no timeout, the request and its run_in_threadpool worker then hang indefinitely. Fix: add '-nostdin' (or stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL), and optionally a timeout that converts TimeoutExpired into RuntimeError. Minor hardening, not a demonstrated vulnerability: ffmpeg sniffs the format from the contents despite the extension whitelist. An 'ffconcat' body in a '.wav' upload is opened by the concat demuxer, but safe=1 confines it to relative files inside local_storage/audio/, and HLS/SDP are not reachable this way in current ffmpeg. Pinning '-f <ext>' before '-i' closes this. There is no evidence that a malformed upload by itself makes ffmpeg stall.

findings.title: Markdown flattener deletes underscores and asterisks inside words (snake_case, __init__, arithmetic)
findings.detail: _MD_EMPHASIS_RE matches `_x_` and `*x*` anywhere, including inside words, and inline code is unwrapped first, so code identifiers get stripped too. Verified: 'Call text_to_speech_file now' -> 'Call texttospeech_file now'; 'Set MAX_TTS_WORDS to 10' -> 'Set MAXTTSWORDS to 10'; 'See `my_var_name` here' -> 'See myvarname here'; '__init__.py' -> 'init.py'; '5*3*2 = 30' -> '532 = 30'. This contradicts the comment at lines 105-107 ("never touches characters with no markdown meaning"; CommonMark does not treat underscores inside a word as emphasis). Technical .md files such as READMEs, which are a main reason to flatten Markdown, get read out with merged words.
findings.suggestion: Add word-boundary lookarounds to the emphasis pattern, for example `(?<![\w*])(\*\*\*|\*\*|\*|___|__|_)(?!\s)(.+?)(?<!\s)\1(?![\w*])`. Add tests for snake_case, __dunder__ and 2*3*4.
findings.verification_note: The core bug is real. I reproduced it read-only against the actual `_strip_markdown_for_speech`. features/audio/text_to_speech.py:115 `_MD_EMPHASIS_RE = (\*\*\*|\*\*|\*|___|__|_)(\S.*?\S|\S)\1` has no word-boundary guards, and line 126 unwraps inline code before line 127 applies emphasis. Confirmed outputs: - 'Call text_to_speech_file now' -> 'Call texttospeech_file now' - 'Set MAX_TTS_WORDS to 10' -> 'Set MAXTTSWORDS to 10' - 'See `my_var_name` here' -> 'See myvarname here' - 'foo_bar_baz' -> 'foobarbaz' The code path is reachable. `extract_text_from_document` (line 507) calls the function for .md/.markdown uploads via features/audio/routes.py:123. The tests at tests/test_text_to_speech.py:424-462 only cover proper emphasis, headings, links, inline code without underscores, fences, lists, HRs and emails. Nothing covers intraword underscores or underscores inside code. Two of the cited examples are wrong as evidence of a CommonMark violation, though: - '5*3*2' is not one. CommonMark allows intraword `*` emphasis ('foo*bar*' renders as foobar), so a renderer would also show 5, an italic 3, then 2. - '__init__.py' is not one either. In CommonMark the `__` before `.` is right-flanking and followed by punctuation, so GitHub renders it as bold "init" followed by ".py". The proposed regex also does not fix '__init__.py'. In memory it still gives 'init.py', while it does fix snake_case and 5*3*2. While checking, I found a second defect in the same regex that the reviewer missed. Because the `\S.*?\S` alternative is tried before the single-character `\S`, single-character emphasis spans across to the next marker and leaves stray asterisks: - '*a* and *b*' -> 'a* and *b' - 'Pick option *A* or *B*.' -> 'Pick option A* or *B.' - '2*3*4 math, and **real** bold' -> '23*4 math, and *real** bold' The leftover '*' characters are exactly what the flattener exists to remove. Severity stays low: it only affects .md uploads to TTS, and the effect is mispronounced or merged words, with no crash or data loss.
findings.corrected:
features/audio/text_to_speech.py:115 (`_MD_EMPHASIS_RE`, applied at line 127 after inline code is unwrapped at line 126) has two real defects, and both are low severity because they only affect .md/.markdown uploads to /tts/extract-text.

(1) Underscores inside words are treated as emphasis. CommonMark does not do this, so the regex contradicts the comment at lines 105-107. It also runs on text that was inside inline code, because backticks are removed first. Results: 'Call text_to_speech_file now' -> 'Call texttospeech_file now', 'Set MAX_TTS_WORDS to 10' -> 'Set MAXTTSWORDS to 10', 'See `my_var_name` here' -> 'See myvarname here'.

(2) The alternation tries `\S.*?\S` before `\S`, so a single-character emphasis such as *A* matches across to the next asterisk and leaves stray markers behind: '*a* and *b*' -> 'a* and *b', 'Pick option *A* or *B*.' -> 'Pick option A* or *B.'.

Not bugs under CommonMark: '5*3*2' (intraword `*` emphasis is valid) and '__init__.py' (GitHub renders it as bold "init" followed by ".py").

Fix: make the underscore delimiters require a non-word character on each side, for example `(?<!\w)(___|__|_)(?!\s)(.+?)(?<!\s)\1(?!\w)`. Try the single-character content before the multi-character content, or use `(?!\s)(.+?)(?<!\s)`. Protect inline-code content from emphasis stripping by handling emphasis before unwrapping code, or by masking code spans. Add tests for snake_case, code spans containing underscores, and '*A* or *B*'. The reviewer's proposed regex fixes snake_case and 5*3*2 but still turns '__init__.py' into 'init.py'.

findings.title: Player query edge cases: bare numbers always use the stale candidate list, and "Dr. Who" over-matches
findings.detail: (1) Any all-digit query is treated as a candidate index (lines 91-93), even when there is no list. "Play 2048" or "play 2026" (default names start with tts_2026-...) returns "There's no previous list..." instead of searching filenames. (2) _last_candidates lives until the next search or pick. After "play music" shows 3 options, an unrelated "play 2" much later still plays the old #2, and the chosen Path is never checked with .exists(), so a deleted file produces a player that 404s. (3) _matches strips a "suffix" whenever the query contains a dot (line 40). Path('dr. who').stem is 'dr', so "play Dr. Who" matches every file whose stem contains 'dr', and 'Meeting 2.5 recap' becomes 'Meeting 2'.
findings.suggestion: If there is no candidate list (or the number is out of range), fall back to a name search for numeric queries. Store a timestamp with _last_candidates and expire it (for example after a few minutes), and check chosen.exists(). In _matches, strip the suffix only when Path(query).suffix.lower() is in AUDIO_EXTENSIONS.
findings.verification_note:
I traced features/audio/player.py and ran a demo against a throwaway temp dir (Python 3.12, repo venv). All three sub-claims hold.

(1) Lines 91-93: any all-digit query goes down the number path. parse_play_command('play 2048') returns {'query': '2048'}. With an empty list, play_audio_file returns "There's no previous list to pick a number from". When a list exists it returns "There's no option 2048 - there are only 3." A real file named 2048.wav can never be found this way. Digit-only names are possible: _build_filename_stem (features/audio/text_to_speech.py:136-155) keeps digits, spaces and dots in user titles. "play 2026" also takes the number path even though default names are tts_2026-....

(2) _last_candidates is cleared only by a successful pick or by a new name search (lines 108, 114, 119, 122). The error branches at lines 102 and 105 leave it in place, and there is no expiry. In the demo, a "dr" search listed 3 files. I then deleted drums.wav and sent "play 2048", which failed and left the list in place. A later "play 2" returned {'status': 'play', 'filename': 'drums.wav'} with no .exists() check, so the /audio/drums.wav player would 404. Mitigation: the app has no delete route, so this case needs the file to be removed outside the app. "play N" picking from the last list is the documented design (docstring, CLAUDE.md), so the missing expiry is a minor robustness gap.

(3) Line 40: Path('dr. who').stem == 'dr' and Path('meeting 2.5 recap').stem == 'meeting 2'. In the demo, "play Dr. Who" returned a choose list of hydrangea.mp3, drums.wav and Dr. Who.wav instead of playing the exact match. "play Meeting 2.5 recap" also listed 'Meeting 2 notes.wav'.

No guard elsewhere prevents these. agent.py:184-186 and core/agent_routes.py:63-67 pass parse_play_command output straight through. Tests in tests/test_audio_tool.py cover the normal number/list flows; test 148 asserts the no-list error only for an explicit number=2. Nothing tests numeric filenames, dotted queries, stale lists or deleted files. Severity "low" is right: the impact is wrong or extra matches and the occasional 404, with no data loss.

findings.title: Dashboard JS: dragging text into the textarea is blocked, and generating speech erases the saved convert format
findings.detail: (1) The textarea's drop handler always calls e.preventDefault() and then extractTextIntoTextarea(e.dataTransfer.files[0]). When the user drags selected text or a link (no files), the browser's built-in text insert is cancelled and extractTextIntoTextarea(undefined) returns immediately, so nothing is inserted. (2) generateSpeech (lines 250-257) calls saveTtsSettings({...}) with a new object that lacks convertFormat, whereas convertFile (line 353) merges with loadTtsSettings(). After a conversion to MP3, generating speech once resets the remembered convert format to WAV.
findings.suggestion: In the dragover/drop handlers, call preventDefault and extract only when e.dataTransfer.types.includes('Files'). In generateSpeech, save with `{...loadTtsSettings(), voice: ..., ...}`.
findings.verification_note:
I traced both parts in the code and both are real. No JS tests exist: tests/test_speech_routes.py only checks the server side of /tts/extract-text.

(1) Text drag into the textarea is blocked. features/audio/static/tts.js:182-195 attaches dragover and drop handlers to #tts-text (features/audio/templates/audio/tts_dashboard.html:55-60), and initTextDropZone() is called at load (tts.js:455). The drop handler always calls e.preventDefault() at line 192, which cancels the browser's default text insertion. It then calls extractTextIntoTextarea(e.dataTransfer.files[0]). When selected text or a link is dragged, dataTransfer.files is an empty FileList, so files[0] is undefined, and extractTextIntoTextarea returns at line 142 (`if (!file) return;`). No other drop handler exists in static/, features/, templates/ or core/. Result: dragging plain text or a URL into the box, or moving a selection inside it, inserts nothing.

(2) generateSpeech erases the saved convert format. generateSpeech (tts.js:250-257) calls saveTtsSettings with a new object that has no convertFormat key, and saveTtsSettings overwrites the whole sessionStorage entry (line 17). convertFile (line 353) merges with loadTtsSettings(), but generateSpeech does not. initTtsControls (line 99) only restores convertFormat if it is present; otherwise the select falls back to its first option, WAV (tts_dashboard.html:147-148). So the sequence "convert to MP3, then generate speech" loses convertFormat. One small clarification: the live select on the current page is not changed. The remembered value is only lost the next time the page loads in the same tab, because sessionStorage is per tab. That does not change the finding.

Low severity is right: these are UX issues only, with no data loss and no server impact. The suggested fixes are correct and local to tts.js: only preventDefault/extract when e.dataTransfer.types includes 'Files', and spread loadTtsSettings() in generateSpeech. Neither touches a cross-file contract.

findings.title: Redundant except branches and stale comments in the audio feature
findings.detail: In all four POST handlers (lines 75-78, 101-104, 126-129, 148-151), `except RuntimeError` returns exactly the same 500 response as the `except Exception` after it, so that branch adds nothing. Several comments and names are stale: routes.py:55 refers to `tools.audio.play_audio_file` (now features.audio.player); tts.js:1-3 says "server picks the backend based on the chosen voice" (Kokoro is the only backend now); tts_dashboard.html:119 has the class typo `tss-field` (audio.css defines .tts-field), so the Convert section misses the field spacing the Play section gets. vulture's audio hits (route handlers, play_audio_file, parse_play_command, describe_play_result, audio_static_files) are all false positives: they are used through decorators, the registry, agent.py and core/agent_routes.py.
findings.suggestion: Remove the `except RuntimeError` branches (or give them a different status if that was the intent), fix the two stale comments, and rename `tss-field` to `tts-field`.
findings.verification_note:
I checked each claim against the code.
- CONFIRMED: In features/audio/routes.py, the `except RuntimeError` branches at lines 75-76, 101-102, 126-127 and 148-149 return the same `JSONResponse({"error": str(e)}, status_code=500)` as the `except Exception` that follows each one, so they do nothing. Removing them changes no behavior. tests/test_speech_routes.py:79-89 expects a 500 when a RuntimeError is raised, and that test would still pass.
- CONFIRMED: routes.py:55 refers to `tools.audio.play_audio_file`. tools/audio.py no longer exists (it was added in 79c96ed and later moved). The function now lives in features.audio.player, which is how tools/registry.py:67, agent.py:12 and core/agent_routes.py:17 reference it.
- CONFIRMED: tts_dashboard.html:119 has `class="tts-collapsible tss-field"`. `tss-field` appears nowhere in CSS or JS, so the class does nothing.
- OVERSTATED: The claimed effect of the typo is wrong. The Convert `<details>` wraps its content in `.tts-collapsible-content` (audio.css:305-310: flex column, gap 16px, margin-top 12px), so it already has its own spacing. The Play `<details>` (line 167) has no such wrapper, which is why it relies on `.tts-field` (flex column, gap 6px). Renaming the class to `tts-field` would add another 6px gap on top of the 12px margin. That is a small layout change, not a fix for missing spacing.
- REFUTED: The tts.js:1-3 comment is not stale. TTS has used only Kokoro since the first commit (79c96ed). "Backend" in the comment means the per-voice Kokoro language pipeline, and the server still chooses that by voice: text_to_speech.py:228-229 runs `lang_code = KOKORO_VOICES[voice_id]["lang_code"]; pipeline = _get_pipeline(lang_code)`. The word choice is loose at worst.
- CONFIRMED: vulture's audio hits are false positives. core/ui.py:13/24/41 uses `audio_router` and `audio_static_files`. agent.py:184-187 and core/agent_routes.py:63-67/102/175 use parse_play_command, play_audio_file and describe_play_result. The routes are registered through decorators.

Severity is low, and this is not a design change.
findings.corrected: Severity is low; this is dead code and cleanup. (1) In features/audio/routes.py, the `except RuntimeError` branches at lines 75-76, 101-102, 126-127 and 148-149 are redundant: the `except Exception` after each one returns the same 500 response. Remove them, or give them a different status if a separate status was intended. The existing test at tests/test_speech_routes.py:79 still passes either way. (2) The docstring at routes.py:55 still names `tools.audio.play_audio_file`. tools/audio.py no longer exists, so it should say `features.audio.player.play_audio_file`. (3) In features/audio/templates/audio/tts_dashboard.html:119, `tss-field` is a typo that matches no CSS rule, so the class does nothing. It has almost no visible effect, because the Convert section gets its spacing from its inner `.tts-collapsible-content` wrapper. Either remove the class or rename it to `tts-field`, knowing the rename adds an extra 6px gap. The tts.js:1-3 comment is not stale. The server does choose the Kokoro language pipeline from the voice (text_to_speech.py:228-229), and TTS has never used anything but Kokoro, so leave that comment alone. The vulture audio hits are all false positives.

findings.title: Times written as '12.30' / '14.00' / '1030' create an event in the year 1230 / 1400 / 1030
findings.detail: `_normalize_time_token` removes '.' and then only recognises H or H:MM. So '12.30' becomes '1230', the regex fails, and the raw '1230' is returned. `_parse_datetime("4 october 1230")` then matches the "%d %B %Y" format (line 52) and reads 1230 as the year. Verified: POST /ask_stream with 'add a meeting on 4 october at 12.30' replies "Event 'Meeting' added from 1230-10-04T00:00:00+00:00 ..." and writes that event to the .ics file. It never appears in the month grid. 'at 14.00' (the standard Norwegian notation) gives year 1400, and 'at 1030' gives year 1030.
findings.suggestion: Accept '.' as a separator (`^(\d{1,2})(?:[:.](\d{2}))?\s*(am|pm)?$`) or accept HHMM. If the token doesn't match, return None so the parse fails, instead of passing the raw digits on to a format that contains %Y. Add parser tests for these inputs.
findings.verification_note:
I traced the code and reproduced the bug. In features/calendar/calendar.py:84, `_normalize_time_token` strips '.', so '12.30' becomes '1230'. The regex on line 85 only accepts H, HH or H:MM. When it doesn't match, line 87 returns the raw token. `_parse_datetime("4 october 1230")` then tries the formats in order. The first one that matches is "%d %B %Y" (line 52), which reads 1230 as the year.

Running parse_create_command directly gives:
- 'add a meeting on 4 october at 12.30' → datetime(1230,10,4,0,0)
- 'at 14.00' → year 1400
- 'at 1030' → year 1030
- '12.30 to 13.30' → start in year 1230, end in year 1330
- '12:30' parses correctly. '2.30pm' returns None (that one fails cleanly).

Nothing stops it before the write. agent.py:174-176 (CLI and /ask_stream) and core/agent_routes.py:49-51 (/ask) call create_event(**cmd) straight away, with no permission prompt. I built the same ics Event in memory without writing a file. It prints "Event added from 1230-10-04T00:00:00+00:00 to 1230-10-04T01:00:00+00:00" and serializes as DTSTART:12301004T000000Z. events_in_month (line 221) filters on the year, so the event never shows up in any month near today.

No test covers this. tests/test_calendar.py only calls create_event with ISO strings. tests/test_agent_flow.py:121 monkeypatches create_event, and no test calls parse_create_command with a dotted or HHMM time.

The suggested fix is sound. Accept [:.] as the separator, or HHMM. When the token doesn't match, return None or raise, so a bare number can't reach a format that contains %Y.
findings.status_note: Times are parsed separately from dates and accept 12.30, 14.00, 1030, 12:30, 2pm and 2.30 pm, so a time can never be read as a year. Tests cover each form.

findings.title: Reversed or past-midnight time range: 500 on /ask_stream and CLI crash; am/pm not carried from end to start
findings.detail: `parse_create_command` (calendar.py:115-125) normalises the start and end tokens separately. 'at 3 to 4pm' silently becomes 03:00-16:00. 'at 2pm to 3', 'at 14 to 12' and 'at 23 to 1' give end < start, and ics' `Event.end` setter (calendar.py:172) raises `ValueError('End must be after begin')`. Nothing on the create-shortcut path catches it. Verified: POST /ask_stream 'add a meeting on 20 october at 2pm to 3' returns HTTP 500 'Internal Server Error'. chat.js has no res.ok check, so the UI shows nothing at all. In the CLI, agent.py:176 raises out of `run_agent`, and the `__main__` loop (agent.py:413) has no try, so the process exits with a traceback. The plain /ask route catches it only because of its outer try.
findings.suggestion: In `parse_create_command`: if only the end token has am/pm, apply it to the start; if the end is still <= start, roll it to the next day or return None. Also wrap `create_event` in the shortcut paths (agent_routes.shortcut_text_response and agent.py:176) so a ValueError becomes an error event or message.
findings.verification_note: I traced the code and reproduced every part of the finding with read-only checks. In features/calendar/calendar.py:115-125, `parse_create_command` runs `_normalize_time_token` on the start and end tokens separately (lines 118-119), so am/pm on one token never carries over to the other. I ran `parse_create_command` and got: 'at 2pm to 3' -> start 14:00, end 03:00; 'at 14 to 12' -> 14:00/12:00; 'at 23 to 1' -> 23:00/01:00; 'at 3 to 4pm' -> 03:00/16:00, a 13-hour event created silently with no error. For the three reversed cases, `create_event` at calendar.py:172 (`event.end = ...`) raises ics' `ValueError('End must be after begin')`. Nothing on the shortcut path catches it. With TestClient (auth overridden), POST /ask_stream 'add a meeting on 20 october at 2pm to 3' returned 500 'Internal Server Error'. The error escapes because `shortcut_text_response` (agent_routes.py:164 -> 51) runs synchronously in the handler, before the StreamingResponse exists. POST /ask returned 200 and showed the error text, but only because of the outer try/except at agent_routes.py:81/147. In static/chat.js, `handleAskStream` (58-102) has no res.ok check. The plain-text 500 body fails `JSON.parse`, which only goes to console.error. `clearStreamUI` has already hidden the cards, so the user sees nothing. On the CLI path, `agent._run_steps('... at 23 to 1', None)` raises the same ValueError from agent.py:176. `run_agent` does not catch it, and the `__main__` loop calls `print(run_agent(user_input))` at agent.py:413 with no try, so the CLI process exits with a traceback. There is no guard anywhere else, and no tests cover reversed or past-midnight ranges: tests/test_calendar.py never calls `parse_create_command`. One mitigating detail: the exception fires before the file write in `create_event` (lines 180-182), so the calendar file is not corrupted. I checked that its mtime did not change. The location (crash surfacing at agent_routes.py:164, root cause in calendar.py:115-125) and the suggested fix are both accurate.
findings.status_note: Ranges follow a 24-hour day: an end before the start is read as the afternoon ("11 to 1" is 11:00-13:00, "2pm to 3" is 14:00-15:00), otherwise as the next day. A pm on the end carries over to the start. Any remaining calendar error becomes a reply instead of a 500 or a CLI crash.

findings.title: Create shortcut matches anywhere in the sentence and skips the 'ask' permission rule, so questions and negations write events
findings.detail: `CREATE_TRIGGER_RE.search` is not anchored. The note and play parsers are deliberately anchored to the start of the message 'to avoid firing on unrelated sentences' (features/audio/player.py:150). Verified: 'did I schedule a meeting on 4 october at 12' and "don't schedule a meeting on 20 october at 12" both return a create command. Both shortcut paths (core/agent_routes.py:49-52, agent.py:174-177) then call `create_event` directly. config/settings.py sets RULES['create_calendar_event'] = 'ask', but that rule is never consulted here, so the calendar file is written with no confirmation.
findings.suggestion: Anchor the trigger to the start of the message (allowing an optional 'please'/'can you'), and reject messages that start with a negation or question word ('did', 'do', "don't", 'is', ...). Alternatively, turn the parsed command into a `planned_first_decision` for create_calendar_event so it still goes through `request_permission`, which keeps the reliability of the shortcut while honouring RULES.
findings.verification_note:
I could not refute it, and I reproduced it.

- **Unanchored trigger.** `CREATE_TRIGGER_RE` (features/calendar/calendar.py:8-11) is `\b(add|schedule|create|book|set ?up)\b.*\b(meeting|...)\b`. It is applied with `.search` at line 106, so it matches anywhere in the message, and nothing rejects questions or negations.
- **Parser output.** Running `parse_create_command` directly returns a create dict for all of these:
  - 'did I schedule a meeting on 4 october at 12'
  - "don't schedule a meeting on 20 october at 12"
  - 'should I book a call on 5 october at 14'
  - 'what did I schedule? the meeting on 4 october at 12'
- **Both callers write without asking.** `core/agent_routes.py:49-51` (`shortcut_text_response`, used by `/ask` at line 91 and `/ask_stream` at line 164) and `agent.py:174-176` (`_run_steps`) call `create_event(**calendar_command)` directly. Neither goes through `request_permission`.
- **End-to-end check.** I replaced `create_event` with an in-memory recorder, so nothing was written to disk. With that in place, `shortcut_text_response("don't schedule ...")` and `list(agent._run_steps('did I schedule ...', {}))` both called `create_event`. The web flow passed a decisions map, but no `PermissionRequired` was raised.
- **The 'ask' rule is skipped.** `config/settings.py:9` sets `RULES['create_calendar_event'] = 'ask'`, but that rule is only read in `core/permission.py:15`, which this shortcut path never reaches.
- **Contrast with the other shortcuts.** The play parser uses an anchored `^\s*play\b` with `.match`, and its docstring (features/audio/player.py:150-153) says it is anchored like `tools/notes.py`'s `parse_note_command` to avoid firing on unrelated sentences.
- **No guard or test covers it.** No test exercises `parse_create_command` with questions or negations; tests/test_calendar.py has no tests for it at all. `test_ui_permission_flow` (tests/test_agent_flow.py:102) uses 'schedule a team sync' with no date, so the parser returns None and the shortcut is never hit. That test's comment also says create_calendar_event 'always requires explicit approval', which the shortcut contradicts.

The location, mechanism and medium severity are accurate: this causes unwanted writes to the local `.ics` file, with no data loss or security exposure. The suggested fix of routing the shortcut through `request_permission` / `planned_first_decision` would change the shortcut's contract, because it would then emit `permission_required`.

findings.title: is_calendar_request swallows create/delete requests and code questions that mention the calendar
findings.detail: The check is just a substring test: 'calendar' plus ('show' or 'my calendar' or "what's on"). It runs before the LLM in both /ask (agent_routes.py:109) and /ask_stream (agent_routes.py:180). Verified True, which opens the grid and does nothing else, for: 'add a dentist appointment to my calendar tomorrow at 3pm' (`parse_create_command` returned None, so no event is created and the LLM never gets the chance to call create_calendar_event), 'put lunch with Bob on 4 october at 12 in my calendar', 'remove the meeting from my calendar', 'show me calendar.js', and 'how does features/calendar/calendar.py show events' (this one should reach the file tools). False negatives: 'what’s on the calendar' (curly apostrophe) and 'open calendar'.
findings.suggestion: Only shortcut when there is no create/delete/edit verb and no file-like token (reuse agent.FILE_TASK_RE). Prefer anchored patterns such as ^(show|open|view)( me)? (my )?calendar or ^what('|’)s on. Add negative tests for the phrases above.
findings.verification_note:
I traced the code and the finding holds. features/calendar/calendar.py:276-281 is only a substring test: 'calendar' in lower(input) AND ('show' or 'my calendar' or "what's on" or 'what is on'). In core/agent_routes.py the web routes check things in this order: shortcut_text_response (note parse, then parse_create_command), then audio_play_result, then is_calendar_request. That last check is at line 109 for /ask and line 180 for /ask_stream. When it returns True, the route returns only the month grid (empty response plus calendar_month/show_calendar), and run_agent/stream_agent are never called.

I ran a read-only python -c in the venv to confirm. Each of these returns None from parse_note_command, parse_create_command and parse_play_command, and True from is_calendar_request:
- 'add a dentist appointment to my calendar tomorrow at 3pm'. CREATE_TRIGGER_RE matches, but CREATE_RANGE_RE and CREATE_SINGLE_RE both need "on <date> at ...", so the parse returns None.
- 'put lunch with Bob on 4 october at 12 in my calendar'. "put" is not a trigger verb.
- 'remove the meeting from my calendar'
- 'show me calendar.js'
- 'how does features/calendar/calendar.py show events'

For all of these, the user sees the calendar grid with no message. No event is created or deleted, and the LLM never gets the chance to use the create_calendar_event registry tool (tools/registry.py:56) or the file tools. Nothing else catches these inputs first: the note and play parsers are anchored to the start of the message, and the create parser fails as described.

The false negatives are also real. 'what’s on the calendar' (curly apostrophe) and 'open calendar' both return False. The impact is small, though: they just go to the LLM, which can call read_calendar, and agent.py:329 turns that result into the grid.

The tests don't cover this. tests/test_calendar.py:55-59 only checks three positive phrasings and one unrelated negative ('weather'), with no create/delete/code-question negatives.

One minor scope note: the CLI (run_agent via python -m agent) never calls is_calendar_request, so only the web /ask and /ask_stream flows are affected. Severity medium fits: create/delete requests sent in the web UI are silently dropped.

findings.title: An LLM-chosen read_calendar opens the grid on the month of the OLDEST event ever stored, and the LLM never sees the events
findings.detail: `read_calendar` returns every event sorted ascending, and `_run_steps` uses `result[0]['date']` for show_calendar, then returns without feeding the result back. Verified with a 2025-03-02 event plus a 2026-10-16 event: stream_agent('do I have any meetings this week?') emits show_calendar {year: 2025, month: 3}. Once any old event exists, every question the LLM routes to read_calendar ('when is my next meeting?', 'anything tomorrow?') opens a stale month. Because the list is intercepted, a text answer is impossible. It also means a skill cannot use read_calendar: the weekly-report skill had to drop its calendar step, because the run ended on the calendar grid with no report.
findings.suggestion: Give read_calendar optional year/month (or start/end) parameters and say so in its registry description. Then derive show_calendar from the requested range, or fall back to the current month or the first upcoming event. Consider feeding a short text summary back to the LLM for questions, rather than always intercepting.
findings.verification_note:
I traced the code and the finding holds. features/calendar/calendar.py:197-210 `read_calendar()` takes no parameters and returns every stored event sorted by `e.begin`, oldest first. agent.py:329-336 checks the result with `is_calendar_event_list(result)`, sets `first = result[0]`, yields `show_calendar: {year: first["date"].year, month: first["date"].month}` with an empty response, and returns. The result is never added back into `context`, so the LLM never gets to write a text answer.

Nothing stops this from happening:
- read_calendar is risk "low" and has no entry in RULES (config/settings.py), so it runs without asking for permission.
- core/agent_routes.py:180 `is_calendar_request` only catches messages that contain the word "calendar" plus "show", "my calendar" or "what's on". "do I have any meetings this week?" or "when is my next meeting?" skip that shortcut and go to stream_agent / run_agent.
- static/chat.js:116-117 passes the year/month straight to `loadCalendarMonth`, which fetches /calendar/month for that month.

I reproduced it read-only. I swapped `_load_calendar` for an in-memory Calendar holding a 2025-03-02 and a 2026-10-16 event, used canned LLM decisions (needs_tools, then read_calendar), ran the real `execute_tool`, and stubbed `log_event`. `stream_agent('do I have any meetings this week?')` yielded `{'event': 'final_response', 'response': '', 'show_calendar': {'year': 2025, 'month': 3}}`. `run_agent('when is my next meeting?')` returned `{'show_calendar': {'year': 2025, 'month': 3}}`.

Tests miss it. tests/test_agent_flow.py:44-99 mocks `execute_tool` with a single October 2026 event, so the oldest event and the relevant month happen to be the same.

The trigger condition is certain to occur over time. The live local_storage/my_calendar.ics currently holds only October 2026 events, and nothing ever deletes events. So from November on, every LLM-routed calendar question will open October or an even older month.

Two minor related points, not needed for the verdict. The CLI's `print(run_agent(...))` (agent.py:415) prints the raw dict `{'show_calendar': ...}` instead of any event information. And `read_calendar()` accepts no arguments, so if the LLM passes any (for example a date range), `execute_tool` raises a TypeError, and agent.py:308 does not catch it.

Medium severity is reasonable. The user can still page forward through months, but they never get an answer to their question. The location (agent.py:329-336, with `first = result[0]` at line 330) is correct, and so is the mechanism.

findings.title: Dates without a year from the LLM tool and `calendar_target_month` still assume the current year
findings.detail: `_parse_datetime` substitutes `current_year` for any year-less format. Verified on 2026-10-15: 'add a meeting on 5 january at 10' creates the event on 2026-01-05, which is already in the past; 'show my calendar for 5 january' opens Jan 2026. Separately, strptime parses year-less formats against 1900, which is not a leap year, so '29 february' raises before `.replace(year=...)` ever runs. Verified: `strptime('29 February 10:00', '%d %B %H:%M')` gives 'day is out of range for month'. So in a leap year such as 2028, 'on 29 february at 10' still can't be parsed.
findings.suggestion: Parse year-less strings with a leap placeholder year (e.g. append ' 2000' and add %Y to the format), then set the year to the current year. For creation, if the result is already in the past, roll forward to next year.
findings.verification_note:
I couldn't refute either part; both reproduce as described. features/calendar/calendar.py:69-71 runs `datetime.strptime(text, fmt)` and then, for formats with no %Y, calls `dt.replace(year=current_year)`. Nothing rolls a past date forward. The parse_create_command callers in agent.py:174-176 and core/agent_routes.py:49-51 call create_event(**cmd) with no check, and calendar_target_month (calendar.py:298) has none either.

Reproduced with read-only `python -c` in the venv (Python 3.12.14) on 2026-10-15:
- `parse_create_command('add a meeting on 5 january at 10')` returns start=2026-01-05 10:00, a date already in the past. The range form ('... at 10 to 11') does the same.
- `calendar_target_month('show my calendar for 5 january')` returns (2026, 1).
- `datetime.strptime('29 February 10:00', '%d %B %H:%M')` raises 'day is out of range for month', because the year-less parse defaults to 1900, which is not a leap year. As a result, `_parse_datetime('29 february 10:00')` raises 'Unable to parse date/time', while '29 february 2028 10:00' parses fine.
- `parse_create_command('add a meeting on 29 february at 10')` returns None, so the shortcut is silently skipped and the request falls through to the LLM tool loop.
- `calendar_target_month('show my calendar for 29 february')` silently returns the current month, (2026, 10).

The leap-day failure happens before `.replace(year=...)` runs, so it fails in leap years like 2028 too. The only test, tests/test_calendar.py:67-69, asserts just `month == 5` for '17 may', so neither problem is covered.

One small caveat: opening a past month for "show my calendar for 5 january" is arguably acceptable for viewing. The clearer harm is in event creation (silently booking in the past) and in the Feb 29 failure. Medium severity is reasonable.
findings.status_note:
In the chat shortcut, a past date without a year now asks the user to say it again with the year, and 29 February parses in leap years. Still open: `_parse_datetime`, used by `create_calendar_event` from the LLM and by `calendar_target_month`, still assumes the current year and can't parse 29 February without a year.

Originally reported as: Dates without a year always use the current year (past dates, Dec->Jan) and Feb 29 never parses

findings.title: calendar_target_month ignores ordinals and bare month names
findings.detail: `\b\d{1,2}\b` cannot match '4th' (there is no word boundary between '4' and 'th'), and a month name without a day isn't recognised at all. Verified: "what's on my calendar on 4th october" and 'show my calendar for december' both return the current month. The `[a-z]*` suffix is also loose: '3 decisions' is read as December 3. `parse_create_command` does accept ordinals, so the two parsers are inconsistent.
findings.suggestion: Strip ordinal suffixes first, as `_parse_datetime` does. Match full or abbreviated month names with a word boundary (e.g. `\b(jan(uary)?|feb(ruary)?|...)\b`), and accept a month name with no day, plus 'next month'.
findings.verification_note:
I checked this by reading the code and running it. features/calendar/calendar.py:292-295 uses `(\b\d{1,2}\b)\s+(jan|...|dec)[a-z]*`. There is no word boundary between '4' and 'th', so ordinals never match. The regex also has no day-free branch, so a bare month name falls through to `datetime.now()`.

I ran it with non-October months, since the current month is October:
- "what's on my calendar on 4th may" returned (2026, 10).
- "show my calendar for the 4th of may" returned (2026, 10).
- "show my calendar for december" returned (2026, 10).
- "show my calendar for may 4" returned (2026, 10). Month-first order also fails, which the finding does not mention.
- "show my calendar for 4 may" returned (2026, 5), which is correct.
- "what is on my calendar 3 decisions" returned (2026, 12). The loose `[a-z]*` suffix is real, but it only applies after is_calendar_request passes, so the input is contrived.
- parse_create_command("add a meeting on 4th may at 3pm") parses correctly to May 4, because `_parse_datetime` strips ordinals at line 36. So the two parsers really do disagree.

Callers are core/agent_routes.py:110 (/ask) and :181 (/ask_stream). Both use the result directly as the month the calendar opens on, and nothing upstream normalises the input. The tests (tests/test_calendar.py:62-69) cover only the default case and "17 may", so ordinals, month-first order and bare months are untested.

Severity low is right. The month grid has Previous/Next buttons (features/calendar/static/calendar.js:115,125), so the user can recover by clicking. The docstring only promises the day+month form ("17 may"), so this is a limited parser rather than a crash or data bug. Still, the shortcut silently shows the wrong month for very common phrasings.

findings.title: Local wall-clock times are stored and reported as UTC
findings.detail: Naive datetimes are assigned to ics/arrow, which treats them as UTC. Verified: the file contains DTSTART:20261020T120000Z for a 12:00 local meeting, and the confirmation reads 'added from 2026-10-20T12:00:00+00:00'. Inside the app it round-trips consistently, because `event_iso` uses .naive and JS parses that as local. But if the .ics is opened in a real calendar app, events shift by the UTC offset (+2h in Oslo). An imported .ics with real Z times is bucketed and displayed by UTC date and time, so late-evening events land on the wrong day.
findings.suggestion: Attach the local timezone (e.g. `arrow.get(dt, tzinfo='local')` or `dt.astimezone()`) when creating events. In `event_iso`, convert to local time (`.to('local').naive`) instead of using `.naive`. Format the confirmation message without the offset.
findings.verification_note:
I traced the code and reproduced the bug in memory, with no file writes, using ics 0.7.3 and arrow 1.4.0 on a machine set to Europe/Oslo (CEST +0200).

1. **Naive local times are stored as UTC.** `create_event` (features/calendar/calendar.py:169-174) assigns the naive datetime from `_parse_datetime` to `event.begin`. ics/arrow treats it as UTC. For a 12:00 meeting, `e.begin` comes back as `2026-10-20T12:00:00+00:00` with tz UTC, and the serialized file says `DTSTART:20261020T120000Z` / `DTEND:20261020T130000Z`.
2. **The confirmation message shows the UTC offset.** Line 184 interpolates the Arrow object, so it reads "added from 2026-10-20T12:00:00+00:00". `read_calendar` (lines 193-198) also passes these UTC Arrow objects to the LLM.
3. **The real file has the same pattern.** `local_storage/my_calendar.ics` contains `DTSTART:20261004T120000Z` / `DTEND:20261004T140000Z`, which matches the parser's "on 4th october at 12 to 14" example. The `20261020` date in the finding is the reviewer's in-memory example, not what is in the file; the mechanism is the same.
4. **Inside the app it stays consistent.** `event_iso` (line 247) returns `value.naive.isoformat()`, which is `2026-10-20T12:00:00`. calendar.js (lines 28 and 45) does `new Date(isoString)`, which reads an offset-less ISO string as local time. So the app's own events show the wall-clock time the user typed.
5. **Imported UTC events land on the wrong day.** An event with `DTSTART:20261031T230000Z` parses as month 10 and `event_iso` gives `2026-10-31T23:00:00`. `events_in_month` (line 232) puts it in October and the grid shows it on Oct 31 at 23:00, but in Oslo it is Nov 1 at 00:00. An event written as `DTSTART;TZID=Europe/Oslo:...` is handled correctly (`+02:00`, wall clock kept), so only UTC/Z events from outside are affected.
6. **No guard or test catches it.** Nothing in the code converts timezones. `tests/test_calendar.py:90` only checks that the start string begins with `2026-05-17T10:00`, which passes either way.

**Caveats (they don't refute the finding):**
- The app has no import or export feature. Both external symptoms need the user to open `local_storage/my_calendar.ics` in another calendar app, or to drop an outside .ics file there. The multi-calendar merge in `_load_calendar` (lines 150-158) suggests outside files are expected.
- Low severity is right.
- The suggested fix changes stored data. Events already saved as local-time-written-as-Z, like the Oct 4 12:00Z one, would move by the UTC offset once `event_iso` converts to local, so it needs a migration or a note. That makes it a storage-contract change (is_design_change=true).

findings.title: Non-atomic truncate-and-rewrite; one damaged .ics breaks every calendar entry point
findings.detail: `create_event` opens the real file with 'w' and streams `serialize_iter()` into it, so an interrupted write leaves a truncated file. The load-modify-write also races between a CLI and a web process (lost update). Verified: with a truncated file, `month_payload`, `read_calendar` and `create_event` all raise ics ParseError, so GET /calendar/month returns 500. calendar.js `loadCalendarMonth` doesn't check res.ok, so the grid fails silently. Contrast tools/files.py, which keeps a .bak.
findings.suggestion: Write to a temp file in the same directory and `os.replace()` it over the original, optionally keeping a .bak. In `loadCalendarMonth`, check res.ok and show an error instead of throwing.
findings.verification_note:
I checked each claim against the code and reproduced the failures against a scratchpad copy of the file. The live calendar was not touched.

- **Non-atomic write:** at features/calendar/calendar.py:181-182, `create_event` opens CALENDAR_FILE with "w", which truncates it first, then calls `f.writelines(calendar.serialize_iter())`. There is no temp file, no `os.replace` and no lock.
- **Race between processes:** `_load_calendar()` runs at line 162 and the rewrite at line 181, with nothing coordinating them. If the CLI and the web server both add an event at the same time, the last writer wins and the other event is lost.
- **Damaged file breaks every entry point:** I wrote two events, then truncated the file at every possible byte offset. At 314 of 483 offsets, `month_payload`, `read_calendar` and `create_event` all raise `ics` ParseError (for example "Expected END:VEVENT, got END:"). `_load_calendar` re-raises anything that isn't the "Multiple calendars" error (line 159).
- **The endpoint returns 500:** with `is_logged_in` overridden, TestClient GET /calendar/month?year=2026&month=10 on a damaged file returns 500 with text/plain "Internal Server Error".
- **The grid fails silently:** features/calendar/static/calendar.js:31-35 calls `fetch` and then `res.json()` without checking `res.ok`. On a 500, `res.json()` hits the plain-text body and throws, so the promise rejects unhandled and the card never renders. The prev/next handlers and the initial-load call at line 141 don't catch it either.
- **The .bak contrast holds:** tools/files.py:331 writes `<path>.bak` before overwriting.

**What the finding understates:** the other 169 truncation points, including a 0-byte file, parse without error and quietly drop events. The next `create_event` then saves that loss for good. A 0-byte file is the most likely result for a small calendar like the current 514-byte local_storage/my_calendar.ics, because a write that small is buffered until close. So an interrupted write often loses data silently rather than raising ParseError. That makes the case for an atomic write stronger, not weaker.

**The fix is safe:** writing a temp file in the same directory and then `os.replace` changes no cross-file contract and breaks nothing. Low severity is reasonable for a single-user local app.

findings.title: 'Would you like to see your calendar?' invites a reply the app cannot handle
findings.detail: Both create shortcuts (agent_routes.py:52 and agent.py:177) end with this question. There is no conversation history (`_run_steps` starts a fresh context every time), and 'yes' is not a calendar request, so the reply goes to `try_local_answer('yes')` with no context and gets a random answer.
findings.suggestion: Emit show_calendar for the created event's month alongside the confirmation, or drop the question. If the question stays, track the pending offer (as player._last_candidates does) so 'yes' is understood.
findings.verification_note: I traced the code path and the bug holds. Both create shortcuts end their reply with the question: core/agent_routes.py:52 (shortcut_text_response, used by /ask and /ask_stream) and agent.py:177 (_run_steps, used by the CLI and stream_agent). Nothing carries state from one request to the next. static/chat.js:132 posts only the form, which has a single `input` field. Both routes pass only user_input. _run_steps builds `context = f"User request: {user_input}\n"` from scratch, and the CLI loop in agent.py (`__main__`) calls run_agent on each line on its own. Unlike player._last_candidates, no pending-offer state is stored. A reply like 'yes' gets past every shortcut: parse_note_command, parse_create_command (CREATE_TRIGGER_RE needs add/schedule/... plus meeting/event/...), parse_play_command, and is_calendar_request (features/calendar/calendar.py:276-281 needs the word 'calendar'). needs_tools('yes') is False, so the reply goes to try_local_answer. I checked this by running _run_steps with query_llm mocked out. For 'yes', 'Yes please', 'sure', 'yes, show it' and 'ok show me', every shortcut returned None. For 'yes' the only LLM prompt sent ended with 'User question: yes' and nothing about the calendar, and the output was just a status event followed by the model's final_response. No test covers this; the phrase appears nowhere in tests/. One more detail: in CLI mode there is no month-grid calendar to show at all, so the question makes even less sense there. Severity low, a UX problem with no data corruption. The location and mechanism in the finding are accurate.
findings.status_note: The reply no longer asks "Would you like to see your calendar?". The calendar opens on the new event's month with its day highlighted.

findings.title: GET /calendar/month silently replaces an invalid month instead of rejecting it
findings.detail: `calendar_month(year: int = None, month: int = None)` accepts any int, and `month_payload` swaps an out-of-range month for the current month but keeps the given year. Verified: ?year=2020&month=13 returns {year: 2020, month: 10} with 200. Non-int input correctly returns 422. The year has no bounds either (0 becomes the current year via `or`).
findings.suggestion: Use `Query(None, ge=1, le=12)` for month and a sane range for year, so bad input returns 422 instead of a different month than the one asked for.
findings.verification_note: The behaviour described is accurate, but the location is wrong: there is no features/routes.py. I checked the code and called the endpoint through TestClient with the auth dependency overridden. Today's date is 2026-10-15. Results: ?year=2020&month=13 returned 200 {year:2020, month:10}. month=-1 and month=0 also fell back to the current month (10) while keeping the given year. year=0 became 2026 because of `year or now.year`. year=-5 and year=99999 came back unchanged with 200. year=abc returned 422. The handler is `calendar_month(year: int = None, month: int = None)` at features/calendar/routes.py:17-19 and has no Query bounds. The silent fallback happens in month_payload at features/calendar/calendar.py:258-259. The suggested fix breaks nothing. The only real client is features/calendar/static/calendar.js:31-33. Its prev/next code (around lines 116-132) wraps month and year itself and never sends an out-of-range month. The initial values come from calendar_target_month (calendar.py:284-302) and the chat show_calendar event, and both always produce valid datetime months. tests/test_calendar.py only uses valid params or no params, and `Query(None, ge=1, le=12)` still allows the no-param default. That same point limits the impact: the bad behaviour only shows up with hand-built URLs, so low severity is correct. One thing to know: loadCalendarMonth does not check res.ok, so a 422 would render a broken card. The UI never sends invalid values, so this doesn't matter in practice.
findings.corrected: features/calendar/routes.py:17-19 (not features/routes.py): `calendar_month(year: int = None, month: int = None)` accepts any int. month_payload at features/calendar/calendar.py:258-259 then quietly swaps an out-of-range month (13, 0, -1) for the current month but keeps the given year. year=0 becomes the current year because of `year or now.year`, and other year values such as -5 or 99999 are not bounded. Verified: ?year=2020&month=13 returns 200 {year:2020, month:10}, and non-int input returns 422. The impact is low because the only client (features/calendar/static/calendar.js) wraps month and year itself and never sends out-of-range values, so this only affects hand-built requests. Suggested fix: `Query(None, ge=1, le=12)` for month and a sane `ge`/`le` range for year, so bad input gets a 422. Optionally, month_payload could raise instead of substituting. Nothing currently depends on the substitution.

findings.title: No tests for parse_create_command / _normalize_time_token / _parse_datetime
findings.detail: None of the parser functions are tested anywhere in tests/ (verified by grep). The high and medium parser bugs above ('12.30' read as a year, am/pm, reversed ranges, year rollover, questions or negations firing the trigger) would each be caught by a one-line test. Titles are also always generic: 'add a dentist appointment ...' is saved as 'Appointment' (calendar.py:109-113).
findings.suggestion: Add parametrised tests for the parser covering the inputs listed in the other findings. Consider extracting the text between the trigger verb and 'on' as the event title.
findings.verification_note:
The premise holds up. None of tests/*.py calls parse_create_command, _normalize_time_token or _parse_datetime by name. tests/test_calendar.py:53-69 covers only is_calendar_request and calendar_target_month. A few of these functions do run as a side effect of other tests:
- _parse_datetime runs through create_event('...', '2026-05-17 10:00') and calendar_target_month('17 may'), so the ISO and 'd month' formats get exercised.
- parse_create_command runs once through test_agent_flow.py:115 ('schedule a team sync'), but only on the path that returns None because there is no date.

No test asserts parser output, and _normalize_time_token never runs at all.

I called parse_create_command (features/calendar/calendar.py:100-141) directly and confirmed the bugs the finding cites:
- 'add a meeting on 4th october at 12.30' gives start=datetime(1230,10,4,0,0). The '.' is stripped to '1230', which fails the time regex and is then matched as %Y by '%d %B %Y'.
- 'at 2 to 4pm' gives a start of 02:00.
- 'at 14 to 12' gives end before start.
- 'can you not add a meeting ...' still creates an event.

The title claim is also correct. Lines 109-113 pick the first word from TITLE_KEYWORDS that appears in the text, so 'add a dentist appointment on 4th october at 12 to 14' gets title 'Appointment'. Titles are always one of six generic words, or 'Meeting' by default.

Adding parametrised parser tests changes no contract and breaks nothing. Pulling the title from the text between the trigger verb and 'on' stays inside parse_create_command's existing return shape (title/start/end kwargs for create_event), so callers in agent.py:174 and core/agent_routes.py:49 are unaffected. Severity 'low' and the location are reasonable.
findings.status_note: tests/test_calendar.py now covers `parse_create_command`: dotted, compact and am/pm times, ranges, relative days, weekdays, past dates, 29 February and the error replies.

findings.title: The desktop launchers bind the server to 0.0.0.0
findings.detail: SessionMiddleware is constructed with secret_key="THIS_SECRET", and that string is committed to the repo. desktop/start_agent_ui.fish:17 and desktop/start_agent_ui.bat:9 start uvicorn with --host 0.0.0.0. Starlette session cookies are base64 JSON signed with itsdangerous using that secret. Any host on the LAN can therefore sign {"authenticated": true} and skip /login (core/auth.py:11-14 only checks request.session). From there it can POST /ask with permission_action=write_file&permission_decision=y and approve its own high-risk tool calls, which lets it write arbitrary project files.
findings.suggestion: Read SESSION_SECRET from the environment (load_dotenv already runs in core/ui.py). Refuse to start if it is unset, or generate a random secret per process. Make the launchers bind 127.0.0.1 unless LAN access is explicitly wanted.
findings.verification_note:
I couldn't refute it, and I reproduced the bypass. The cited lines are all accurate. core/ui.py:34 sets `secret_key="THIS_SECRET"`, and core/ui.py is tracked in git. desktop/start_agent_ui.fish:17 and desktop/start_agent_ui.bat:9 both run `uvicorn core.ui:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000`, and the user's desktop entry (desktop/agent0-ui.desktop) launches that fish script, so the LAN can reach the app in normal use. The only auth gate is core/auth.py:11-14, which checks `request.session.get("authenticated") == True`, and Starlette's SessionMiddleware signs base64 JSON with itsdangerous TimestampSigner(secret_key).

To test it, I used TestClient against core.ui:app. GET /calendar/month without a cookie returned 303 to /login. With a cookie built by `TimestampSigner("THIS_SECRET").sign(b64encode(b'{"authenticated": true}'))`, the same request returned 200 with real calendar events, and GET /logout also returned 200.

Once past login, the attacker is treated as the user. On POST /ask, create_permission_decisions (core/agent_routes.py:27-34) turns `permission_action`/`permission_decision` form fields into `{action: True}`, and request_permission (core/permission.py:24-27) honours that without further checks. So the attacker can approve the "ask" actions write_file, edit_file and extract_inline_scripts (config/settings.py RULES).

Two details are less direct than the finding says, but neither weakens it:
- The attacker doesn't pass tool arguments directly. The LLM picks them from the attacker's prompt. The exception is extract_inline_scripts, which planned_first_decision in agent.py:94-106 triggers deterministically.
- Writes are limited to the project directory by tools/files.py `_safe_path`. That still covers agent.py and other code files. Their changes take effect on the next restart, since the launcher doesn't use --reload.
